title: Supreme Court Quashes Yes Bank's Rs 8,415 Crore AT-1 Write-Off; Shares Slide
excerpt: The court upheld the Bombay High Court's order restoring the AT-1 bonds written down in the 2020 rescue, reviving the liability for Yes Bank and the coupons for bondholders.
body:
• The Supreme Court on October 15 set aside Yes Bank's write-off of Rs 8,415 crore in AT-1 bonds, upholding the Bombay High Court's 2023 order quashing it.
  • For bondholders: the bonds written down to zero in March 2020 are restored in law, and annual coupon payments continue in line with the bonds' information memoranda.
  • For shareholders: Yes Bank shares fell as much as 7.8% intraday to Rs 19.55 after the ruling, as the bank faces a revived liability it had removed from its books in 2020.
  • The court held the bank's Administrator acted beyond his powers: the final reconstruction scheme, notified March 13, 2020, had dropped the draft clause proposing the write-down.

Yes Bank shares slid sharply after the Supreme Court set aside the bank's Rs 8,415 crore write-off of Additional Tier-1 (AT-1) bonds, ending a six-year legal fight over losses imposed on bondholders during the lender's 2020 rescue. A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Augustine George Masih on Thursday upheld the Bombay High Court's January 2023 judgment quashing the write-down and dismissed appeals by Yes Bank, the Reserve Bank of India and the Centre, according to Live Law. The stock fell as much as 7.8% intraday to Rs 19.55, TradingView News reported.

What AT-1 Bonds Are

AT-1 bonds are perpetual debt instruments — they have no maturity date — that banks issue to count toward their regulatory capital. In exchange for a higher coupon than ordinary bonds, investors accept that the bonds are designed to absorb losses: if a bank's capital falls below a specified threshold, or regulators judge the bank to be at the point of non-viability, the bonds can be written down or converted, behind depositors and senior creditors in the repayment order. That loss-absorption feature is precisely what was invoked at Yes Bank in 2020 — and what the court has now held was invoked without legal authority.

How the Write-Off Happened

Yes Bank issued the bonds in two tranches: Rs 3,000 crore on December 23, 2016, and Rs 5,415 crore on October 18, 2017. By December 31, 2019, its Common Equity Tier 1 ratio had fallen to 0.6%, against a regulatory requirement of 7.375%. The government imposed a moratorium on March 5, 2020, and the RBI superseded the board and appointed an Administrator. A draft reconstruction scheme published on March 6 proposed permanently writing down the AT-1 bonds — but that clause was omitted from the final Yes Bank Limited Reconstruction Scheme, 2020, notified on March 13. The Administrator nevertheless wrote the bonds down to zero the following day, March 14, relying on the RBI's Master Circular on Basel III capital regulations.

Why the Court Struck It Down

The court held that the government had consciously chosen to leave the bonds untouched after investors objected to the draft clause, and that a write-down, if it was to happen, had to occur before the reconstruction scheme took effect. The Administrator, it held, acted on an erroneous belief that his power survived the scheme, and his action was ultra vires — beyond the powers conferred on him. The bench also criticised the RBI for allowing the bank's capital ratio to fall to 0.6% and held that investors should not bear the consequences of administrative lapses. It clarified that annual coupon payments on the bonds remain unaffected and must continue in accordance with the information memoranda.

"If the appellants' arguments were to be accepted, the Reconstruction Scheme would be akin to a half-baked pie."

— Supreme Court bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Augustine George Masih

Impact on Bondholders and Shareholders

For bondholders — institutions and retail investors whose holdings were extinguished in 2020 — the ruling restores the Rs 8,415 crore claim and the coupon stream attached to it, nearly five months after the court reserved judgment on May 20. For shareholders, the cost runs the other way: a liability the bank treated as gone since 2020 returns to its books, which is why the stock sold off on the verdict. Yes Bank had earlier said any financial liability from the decision would be recognised in the relevant future reporting period and that it did not expect a material financial impact — a claim investors will now test against the bank's next results. The government had warned during the case that nearly Rs 1 lakh crore of AT-1 bonds are outstanding across the banking system, so the ruling's reasoning on when a write-down is lawful will be read closely well beyond Yes Bank.
